newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Sick European car industry needs surgery.
newsitem.headline: Sick European car industry needs surgery.

text.p: For Europe's car industry to regain financial health, more workers must be fired and factories must close.
As the European industry gathers here for the annual car show, that is the bitter recipe that experts say is needed to correct the woes of an industry that is simply making too many cars.

Others say this cull of production will take the form of long promised consolidations and mergers, with the weaker of the big six mass car makers finally losing their independence and succumbing to takeover. This would deliver an industry where the major players had market shares approaching 20 percent, but it couldn't avoid the pain of closures.

In 1996 Germany's Volkswagen was market leader in western Europe with 17.2 percent, followed by General Motors Europe's Opel and Vauxhall brands with 12.5 percent, France's Peugeot Citroen (11.9 percent), Ford (11.6), and Fiat of Italy (11.2). Renault of France brought up the rear with 10.1 percent.

"It's tough to generalise, but most manufacturers have got one plant too many, and current volumes and price levels make it difficult for the sums to add up for anyone," said John Lawson, automotive analyst at investment bank Salomon Brothers.
"A 10 percent cut, (in output capacity) that would get you back to healthy margins from their current unhealthy level," Lawson said.
Recent news suggests that the car makers are gritting their teeth and starting to take tough decisions on production.

In January, Ford said it would slash 980 jobs at its Halewood, England plant. On Thursday last week, Renault announced it would close a factory at Vilvoorde, Belgium, with the loss of 3,100 jobs. The political storm following both these actions underlines why car companies are reluctant to take these tough decisions.
Much more needs to be done, but time is running out. Unless companies take decisions now, it will taken for them by the next economic downturn in the this relentlessly cyclical industry.

"We will see the next downturn in two to three years, when we will see a temporary downturn in sales of up to 20 percent, 15 to 20 percent, it must be at least 15 percent," said Karel Williams, director of graduate studies at Manchester University in north-west England.

To be sure, mainstream forecasting companies don't share this vision. They all expect fairly gentle increases in sales over the next five years. DRI-McGraw Hill for example expects car sales in western Europe to more or less steadily rise to 14.4 million in 2001 from about 13 million this year.
But forecasters were caught short by the sudden 15 percent or two million dive in sales in 1993 to 11.3 million.

"In the next downturn, there will be substantial rationalisation involving members of the big six. Fiat and Peugeot Citroen are most likely to be bought. And what does Renault do next? It's losing masses of money," Williams said.
Garel Rhys, professor of motor industry economics at the Cardiff Business School says this overproduction problem will be addressed by plant closures, joint ventures and mergers.
"There have been a huge number of small mergers in Europe, but reality is closing in on the big six, they've been trying to stave off the evil day," Rhys said.
Rhys pointed out that Ford and Fiat came mighty close to merging 10 years ago.

"If that had happened, that would have provoked changes. The others wouldn't have been able to face up to operating without a 20 percent share. You only need one movement and the whole thing would change," Rhys said.
Rhys sees another possible scenario to trigger this action.

"If VW goes a bit further, reaches 20 percent in about five years, that could provoke a reaction. But that raises tough questions. How do you put the other ones together without destroying them? Peugeot and Renault, their philosophies are so utterly different. The synergy problem would be absolutely immense," said Rhys.

"The idea that you need fewer players is beguiling. But when you start talking about combining companies of these sizes and complexity; the bottom line though is restructuring is inevitable," Rhys said.
If some companies are perceived as vulnerable, who would be the predators?
Williams looks to General Motors and Ford.

"The two American players must be interested in what they could buy. After all, GM bought (Swedish niche producer) Saab and Ford has (British luxury maker) Jaguar. And Ford came close to buying Fiat - that stalled on whose factories were going to close. With (Jac) Nasser in charge will that be a really big issue?" Williams said.
Nasser, with a reputation for not shying from tough decisions, recently took charge of Ford Europe for the second time.
"Ford is prepared to close anything that it has too," Williams said.
